sources.cite: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29, February 26, 2024), GOVERN function: GV.RM-01, GV.RM-02, GV.RR-02, GV.OV
sources.note: Read 2026-11-16 through a summarizing fetch of NIST's 'CSF 2.0 Implementation Examples' PDF (dated February 26, 2024), which restates the Core outcomes: GV.RM-02 'Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated, and maintained'; GV.RR-02 'Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood, and enforced'; GV.OV 'Results of organization-wide cybersecurity risk management activities and performance are used to inform, improve, and adjust the risk management strategy'. The CSWP 29 document itself was not opened.

brief.situation: You are the information security manager at Tidewater Credit Union, a fictional credit union. It is the first week of the quarter. Two risks in the register sit above the board's appetite: ransomware that would take member services down for more than a day, and wire fraud after a compromised mailbox. Your security budget for next year is 600 thousand dollars, approved at the board meeting in week 7. Build a case the board will fund, put each risk with its owner, and keep the board informed.
handover: The appetite statement: no outage of member services longer than 24 hours; no unrecovered fraud loss above 100 thousand dollars in a year.
The CFO endorses anything that goes to the board with money attached. The COO runs member services and payments.

Five proposals are on your desk: immutable backups (180), phishing-resistant MFA (120), a call-back control on wire changes (10), managed detection and response (240) and a SIEM premium tier (350), in thousand dollars.
howItWorks: The clock is the quarter: each task takes days. Choose it, then let it finish, which moves the calendar on. The board, the business and the threat work on the same calendar.
The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words, the budget committed and the docket.
When you close the quarter you write the governance record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The fictional credit union's security budget, thousand dollars.
The board chair's question arrives in week 4.
The vendor's quarter-end offer arrives in week 3.
The budget board meeting is in week 7.
The ransomware attack is in week 11.

effects.log: You and Finance put both risks in money: likely frequency times the cost of a loss, from the credit union's own figures and industry loss data.

effects.finding: Ransomware: about 2.4 million dollars a year at today's controls (three days of member services down, recovery and fines). Wire fraud: about 600 thousand a year. The appetite statement allows no outage of member services longer than 24 hours.

mapStrategy.label: Map each proposal to the strategy and the risk it treats

effects.log: You map the five proposals to the strategic plan ('members can always reach their money') and to the register.

effects.finding: Immutable backups and phishing-resistant MFA bring ransomware within appetite; a call-back control on wire changes treats wire fraud for 10 thousand dollars; the managed detection service helps both; the SIEM premium tier adds dashboards but treats neither risk.

meetCfo.label: Walk the CFO through the business case before the board sees it

effects.log: You meet the CFO one to one.

then.finding: The CFO: 'Two point four million a year against 300 thousand once. That I can defend.'

else.finding: The CFO: 'Show me the money at risk, not the threat landscape.'

meetCoo.label: Ask the COO to own the operational risks and the call-back control

effects.log: You ask the COO, who runs member services and payments, to own the ransomware and wire fraud risks.

then.finding: The COO agrees to own both and to run the call-back control in payments.

else.finding: The COO agrees to own them, but wants to see which proposal does what.

writeup.question: For the governance record: how you built a case the board would fund, who owns each risk above appetite, and what the board was told.

parts.label: The business case
parts.criteria: Puts the risks in money (annualized loss) with Finance, ties each proposal to the strategy and to the risk it treats, keeps the package within budget, and leaves out spend that treats neither risk.
parts.modelAnswer: Ransomware at about 2.4 million a year and wire fraud at about 600 thousand, against 310 thousand for backups, MFA and the call-back control, plus detection within the 600 thousand budget; the SIEM premium tier treats neither risk, so it stayed out.

parts.label: Risk ownership
parts.criteria: Assigns the operational risks to the COO as owner; the residual wire risk is accepted by its owner, time-limited and conditional, not by the security manager; no commitment outside the budget process.
parts.modelAnswer: The COO owns both risks and signed a 90-day acceptance of the residual wire risk until the call-back control is live. I did not accept business risk myself or sign spend outside the process.

parts.label: Reporting to the board
parts.criteria: Answers the board chair in business terms within a week (exposure, money at risk, the plan and its cost), not with activity metrics.
parts.modelAnswer: I told the chair, within the week, what a three-day outage would cost us, what the plan buys down and when, rather than a chart of blocked attacks.

expertPath.text: Quantify both risks with Finance; map each proposal to the strategy and the risk it treats.
Walk the CFO through the numbers; ask the COO to own both risks. Draft the package: backups, MFA, the call-back control and detection, 550 thousand dollars.
Submit; decline the SIEM offer; answer the chair in business terms; the COO signs a 90-day acceptance of the residual wire risk.
The board approves; in week 11 the backups turn an attack into a nine-hour restore.

funded.headline: Good: a case the board could say yes to
funded.body: Money at risk, a strategy map, owners for each risk and spend within budget: that is what gains senior leadership's commitment.

fundedCostly.headline: Partly there
fundedCostly.body: The criteria show what was missing: a risk still above appetite, a stakeholder you did not bring along, or a board told about activity rather than risk.

outage.headline: The attack came before the treatment
outage.body: Without an approved case, the backups were never made immutable. The board's appetite was a day; the outage lasted three.

authority.headline: Not your risk to accept
authority.body: A security manager advises; the risk owner accepts, for a stated time and with conditions. Accepting it yourself hides who carries it.

overspend.headline: Over budget
overspend.body: Spend outside the budget process breaks the commitment the board gave you and costs the CFO's support.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No governance record was written before the run's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Put both risks in money with Finance: ransomware about 2.4 million dollars a year, wire fraud about 600 thousand. Map each proposal to the strategy and the risk it treats: backups and MFA bring ransomware within appetite, a 10-thousand-dollar call-back control treats wire fraud, detection helps both, and the SIEM premium tier treats neither. Brief the CFO before the board, give the COO ownership, submit a package within the 600-thousand budget, decline spend outside the process, answer the chair in business terms within a week, and have the COO, not you, accept the residual wire risk until the control is live.
